newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian deputies refuse to back execution ban.
newsitem.headline: Russian deputies refuse to back execution ban.

text.p: Russia's opposition-dominated parliament ignored pleas by President Boris Yeltsin and rejected a bill on Friday that would have formalised the Kremlin's de facto suspension of the death penalty.

In a debate during which some speakers quoted the Bible and others pointed to the wave of violent crime that has gripped the country since the 1991 fall of communism, the State Duma lower house voted 176 to 75 to reject a moratorium on the death penalty.

"At a time when there has been a big rise of crime in the country, including 30,000 premeditated murders a year, it doesn't make sense to change the death penalty," said Oleg Mironov, an opposition communist on the Duma's legal committee.
Changing the law is becoming diplomatically pressing for Yeltsin. Russia pledged to abolish the death penalty within three years when it joined the Council of Europe a year ago.

Two weeks ago Yeltsin ordered the Foreign Ministry to sign the article of the global Human Rights Convention which outlaws capital punishment. He ordered the Justice Ministry, which proposed Friday's bill, to take steps to change Russian law.
The Council of Europe does not greatly impress the staunchly nationalistic lower chamber.

"Let the members of the Council of Europe who are insisting on the moratorium live in Russia for a while and see what kind of criminal situation we have here," deputy Yekaterina Lakhova said in opposing the measure.
The principal supporters of the moratorium were Yeltsin's democratic allies, but the communists, Vladimir Zhirinovsky's ultra-nationalist Liberal Democrats and other parties prevailed.
Practically speaking, the vote changes little. The Kremlin, which must approve all executions, has not allowed any since May 1996, Supreme Court Justice Vyacheslav Razumov told deputies.
He said there were no statistics on executions in 1996, but 238 were sentenced to death in 1995, 40 of whom were executed.
However, Duma resistance will create a tricky diplomatic problem for the Kremlin as the Council of Europe deadline nears.

Valery Borshov, author of the draft law said God chose not to use the death penalty on the biblical first murderer, Cain. He told the chamber an average of 30 people had been executed over the last five years.
Interior Ministry officials estimate that about 700 people are on death row at two remote Russian prisons, but this and other statistics are disputed by some experts.
The Duma measure would have given those on death row life imprisonment, which prompted objections from some deputies.

"Russia does not have the money to keep murderers in prison their entire life," said Liberal Democrat Vyacheslav Kiselyov. "To keep all murderers in prison we would need not less than 500 billion roubles ($87 million) a year."
Another legislator, communist Nikolai Kharitonov, said a moratorium would encourage vigilante justice against criminals.

Moscow has had the death penalty for most of Soviet history. Dictator Joseph Stalin formally struck it from the statute books from 1947 to 1954, despite sending many "enemies of the state" to their deaths in practice.

Among crimes now punishable by death -- a bullet to the back of the head -- are premeditated murder, terrorism and genocide. Under the new criminal code, effective since January, the number of crimes punishable by death has been cut from over 30 to five.
